note: Track ii-v-i, step 3 (a mix): a major ii–V–I and a minor ii–V–i in one tune, heard as two homes, their roots tapped from a staff whose "line" rings the root of each chord, then named without looking. The tune is written as numerals so it follows the key, which is moves; chords are chord tokens, counted the long way where the staff rings their roots, and the last line opens with {{?key}}.

exercise.title: Major and minor ii–V–I in one tune
exercise.why: A tune can reach its major home with one ii–V–I and its minor home, on La, with another, and the ii chord says early which is coming: minor 7 before the major home, half-diminished before the minor one.

cells.text:
Press Play below to start the backing track: a ii–V–I to {{chord:Imaj7}}, then a ii–V–i to {{chord:vi7}}, round and round. Call out "major" or "minor" as each home chord arrives.
Then listen two bars earlier, to the chord that starts each ii–V: {{chord:ii7}} before the major home, {{chord:vii°7}} before the minor one.

{{chord:Imaj7}} is the 1st chord of the key, built on {{1}}, the major home. {{chord:vi7}} is the 6th chord, built on {{6}}, the minor home.
Press Play below to start the backing track again, slower. On the staff under it, tap the ringed root of each chord as its box lights.
Listen for the two lines moving by the same leaps and ending on the two homes.

Press Play below to start the backing track. Look away from the chord boxes and call out 2, 5 or 1 on each change, and "major" or "minor" on each home chord, then look back to check.
Practice until the first chord of each ii–V tells you which home is coming.
{{?key}}In another key the chords have other names, and the minor home is still built on the 6th note of the major key.
